title: not just a party
hook: a thirteen-year-old, an ancient scroll, then the DJ: which part is the real thing?
tomorrow: an argument for the sake of heaven

segments.voice: Yesterday: the glass, broken right before the cheering. Your line was even in joy, remember. Today, a day many people remember for the DJ.

A thirteen-year-old in a suit that doesn't quite fit, or a dress picked out months ago, stands in front of everyone they know and chants from a handwritten scroll, in Hebrew they've practiced for a year. Then comes the party: the DJ, the candy bar, the chair lifted into the air. So which part was the real thing? Neither one, it turns out, makes it happen.
screen: `THIRTEEN, AND A SCROLL.` → `THEN THE DJ.` → `WHICH PART IS REAL?`

segments.voice: Bar mitzvah means son of the commandment. Bat mitzvah, daughter of the commandment. A mitzvah is one of the things the Torah asks a person to do, and in everyday talk it's also a good deed: that was a real mitzvah. Here's the twist. You don't have a bar or bat mitzvah. You become one. In traditional Jewish law it happens on its own, on a birthday: thirteen for boys, twelve for girls, and many communities mark both at thirteen. Ceremony or no ceremony, party or no party, the day comes. An old teaching lays out a life by ages: five for starting scripture, ten for the rabbis' teachings, thirteen for the commandments. Until then, the responsibility sat with your parents. From that birthday on, it's yours. So the ceremony isn't what makes it happen. It's the first time it's shown in public: called up to read from the Torah, often with a short talk about what that week's reading means to you. And the party? Celebrating a mitzvah with a festive meal is a tradition too. The DJ is newer. Some people take it up as adults, at thirty or sixty or eighty. There's no deadline. And if your own bar or bat mitzvah was the last time you really took part, you're in very good company. Picking it up again years later isn't starting over. It's carrying on.
screen: `SON OR DAUGHTER OF THE COMMANDMENT.` · `YOU BECOME ONE.` · `THIRTEEN FOR THE COMMANDMENTS.` · `SHOWN IN PUBLIC, THEN A MEAL.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. First breath: think back to being twelve or thirteen. Second breath: one thing you're responsible for now that you weren't then. Third breath: let it be yours, without the weight. Just yours.
Mitzvah. A commandment, a good deed, and at a bar or bat mitzvah, a responsibility that becomes yours. Sixth word.
Your line: it's yours now. The day comes on its own; the ceremony just says so out loud. Day six.

screen: `DAY 6 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: AN ARGUMENT FOR THE SAKE OF HEAVEN.`

howItsDone: A Jewish boy becomes bar mitzvah at thirteen and a girl bat mitzvah at twelve in traditional law (thirteen in many communities); many mark it by being called up to read from the Torah, often chanting the week's portion and giving a short talk, followed by a festive meal, and some adults celebrate it later in life.

what it means: becoming responsible for the commandments yourself. it comes with the age; the ceremony shows it.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Avot 5:21: thirteen for the commandments. bar is Aramaic for son; the girls' age of twelve follows the Talmud's rules for adulthood (Niddah 45b).

story.title: the first girl to stand up
story.text: On a Saturday morning in March 1922, in a New York synagogue, a twelve-year-old girl stands up to do something no girl there has done before. Her father, the rabbi, has decided his daughter will mark her coming of age in public, just as boys do. After the regular service, she says the blessing and reads from that week's portion, in Hebrew and in English. She reads from a printed book, not the scroll, standing a careful distance from where the men read. Her name is Judith Kaplan, and hers is often called the first public bat mitzvah in America.
story.source: Judith Kaplan's bat mitzvah, Society for the Advancement of Judaism, New York, 18 March 1922 (Jewish Women's Archive)

wrong.myth: you have a bar or bat mitzvah: the ceremony makes it happen.
